name: Amira Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm an improver carpenter, which is basically a junior who's past the very basics, with a small building co-op that does timber-frame eco houses, the super-insulated kind that barely need heating. Right now we're on six houses at the end of Orchard Lane, outside town. I'm out the door at quarter to seven, and on site it's studwork, fitting the airtight membrane, taping every joint, insulation, window boards. I love that you can see why every detail matters, one gap in the tape and the whole house leaks heat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's hard about it, or wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still slow, and my cuts aren't always clean, so I redo things, which is embarrassing when Gwen, our lead carpenter, is watching. The pay is low because the co-op's tiny and the margins are thin. My partner Leila drives buses, we rent a small terrace on Brook Street, and we've got maybe three weeks of money put aside. I use an AI app every day, though. I take a photo of the drawing and ask it to explain the detail, and at night I use it to revise for my trade certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That would be a bit of an anticlimax for me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic, and anyone who says otherwise was selling something. I'd still tell the younger lads to use it for learning, because it's helped me. Online I'd say the hype money would've been better spent on insulating old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped it would help people like me who left school early catch up faster. But for my actual job, it's fine. People will always need houses that don't leak heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the co-op and get my certificate next spring. I'd keep using the app to study and to check details, maybe pay for the better version if I can find the ten a month. I'd ask the co-op if I can start learning the airtightness testing, the blower-door test, because that's a skill people pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd find the ten a month. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably from my coffee on the way in. I buy one every morning at the garage on the bypass, that's more than ten a month on its own. Leila would laugh, she's been telling me to stop for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you, even if AI stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The co-op folding. We're six people and two bad jobs from closing. That's my real worry, not robots. If that happened there's hardly any other eco builders round here, I'd be back on a big site doing plasterboard.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, not magic, and anyone who says otherwise was selling something. I'd still tell younger lads to use it for learning, and I'd say the hype money should have gone into insulating old houses.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I hoped it would help people who left school early catch up faster. But for my job it's fine: people will always need houses that don't leak heat.
S0.do: Carries on with the co-op and gets her trade certificate next spring. Keeps studying with the AI app, maybe paying ten a month for a better version, and asks to learn airtightness testing.
S0.quote: We're six people and two bad jobs from closing. That's my real worry, not robots.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is already a daily AI user who sees it mostly as a learning aid for people without much schooling. Her real fear is her tiny employer folding, not technology. She looks for a skill with market value, airtightness testing, even in a calm world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the one I actually expect, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's make sure workers get trained and paid for it, not just the bosses. I'd say the co-op is the right model, because we'd share whatever we save. Online I'd probably post about how it's helping me study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me if I move fast, and bad for me if I sit still. I'm junior, my hand skills are average at best, but I'm quick with the tech. If there's a robot that cuts studs to the millimetre, I want to be the one running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd look up which site robots and layout tools are actually being used and do any free online courses. I'd go to Gwen and the co-op meeting and propose we try one, maybe hire a layout robot for one house to see. I'd keep studying for my certificate, because knowing why the detail matters is what lets you check the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a little worry underneath about the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money side worries you. What's the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Courses cost, and I can't lose days of pay to do them. And if I'm the robot person, does the co-op pay me more, or do I just do more? We'd have to vote on it. I'd want it written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Karim, he's a labourer on a big commercial site. He hates anything with a screen. He'd be the one getting moved from task to task till there's nothing left. I'd probably try and drag him onto a course with me.

S1.say: It's coming, so let's make sure workers get trained and paid for it, not just the bosses. A co-op is the right model because we'd share whatever we save.
S1.think: It's good for me if I move fast and bad if I sit still. My hand skills are average at best, but I'm quick with the tech, so if there's a robot cutting studs I want to be the one running it.
S1.do: Researches which site robots and layout tools are in real use within a month and takes free online courses. Proposes the co-op hire a layout robot for one house as a trial, while she keeps studying for her certificate.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some worry underneath about money.
S1.quote: If there's a robot that cuts studs to the millimetre, I want to be the one running it.
S1.fieldNote: Her adaptability makes steady change look like an opening, even though she's junior with weak hand skills. Her worry is practical: course costs and whether extra responsibility brings extra pay. She'd pull her screen-averse brother along with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's different. Even for me, that's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the robots and the AI should be owned by the public, or at least taxed hard, because otherwise a few companies own all the work. I'd be at the protests. I'd share everything about a basic income, I'd be one of those people on your feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being good with AI doesn't help much if AI can do almost everything. My little edge, being quick with the tech, gets swallowed in a year. And with three weeks of savings, I can't spend six months working out a new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd try to get on the side that's still hiring, the companies installing and fixing the robots, even as a junior. I'd join a union for the first time, a proper one, not just the co-op. I'd cut back hard, cancel my coffee, cancel the gym, and Leila and I would talk about moving to the city if that's where the robot work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've been running for a train and someone's moved the platform. But I'd be moving, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said robot-fixing work. What if the robots can fix themselves by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know, honestly. Maybe there's a few years where they still need someone on site to sign it off and carry the blame. I'd take that window. After that it's politics, not my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leila's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses would go driverless, probably even faster than building sites. So we'd both be hit at once, which is the scary part. One of us being okay and the other not is manageable. Both at once isn't.

S2.say: The robots and the AI should be owned by the public, or at least taxed hard, otherwise a few companies own all the work. I'd be at the protests and sharing everything about a basic income.
S2.think: Being good with AI doesn't help much if AI can do almost everything, so my edge gets swallowed in a year. With three weeks of savings, I can't spend six months working out a new plan.
S2.do: Applies straight away to firms installing and fixing robots, even as a junior. Joins a union for the first time, cancels her coffee and gym, and talks with Leila about moving to the city if that's where the work is.
S2.feel: Anxious and rushed, like the platform moved while she ran for the train, but moving rather than frozen.
S2.quote: One of us being okay and the other not is manageable. Both at once isn't.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-comfortable of workers sees her edge vanish in the fast picture, and she says so. She still acts quickly, hunting for a short window of robot installation work. The double hit to her and her bus-driver partner is the core fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can work with, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set things up right if we start now: public training, profits shared, and rules on which jobs go first. I'd be organising, maybe getting the co-op to join a network with other co-ops. I'd say it on site and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it gives me a real window. I'd qualify, then spend three or four years in the robot side of building, getting paid more than now, and save. The end point's still scary, but I'd hit it with some money and some skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get my certificate and do a part-time course in building automation, evening classes, maybe funded by the college. I'd push the co-op to buy one robot and make me responsible for it. And I'd set up a savings pot, a hundred a month, which is a lot for us, so the coffee goes now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly focused. It feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. How would your use of it change in these five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for everything I'm learning, and to price jobs for the co-op, which nobody likes doing. Honestly I'd probably end up the co-op's AI person, which is funny since I'm the most junior. Gwen would hate it and love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids in a few years. I think we'd hold off till we saw how it went, maybe to 2031 itself. That's not a happy thought, but it's honest.

S3.say: Five years is enough to set things up right if we start now: public training, shared profits and rules on which jobs go first. I'd be organising, maybe getting the co-op into a network with others.
S3.think: It gives me a real window. I'd qualify, then spend three or four years on the robot side of building earning more than now and saving, so I'd hit the end point with some money and skills.
S3.do: Gets her certificate and takes an evening course in building automation in the first year. Pushes the co-op to buy one robot with her responsible for it, saves a hundred a month and postpones plans for children.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly focused, because it feels like a plan.
S3.quote: Honestly I'd probably end up the co-op's AI person, which is funny since I'm the most junior.
S3.fieldNote: Five years transforms Amira's outlook from rush to plan, and she sees a chance to earn more on the way. She'd delay having children, which she names as an honest, unhappy choice. Her politics stay collective: co-op networks and shared profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's almost a full career's worth of time for someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, so there's no excuse for a mess. Every worker should get paid time to retrain, and the gains should be shared. I'd say it calmly, as a political argument, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is long enough that I'd get good, move into the tech side, maybe even teach it to other builders. The ending is the same, I'm not daft, but there'd be time for the politics to catch up too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my certificate, do the automation course over two years, and push for the co-op to bring in robots slowly, with a vote on how the time saved is shared. I'd join the union and the local co-op network. And I'd try to get six months of savings over five years, which is about what we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the very back, but mostly curious. I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might teach it. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like evening sessions at the college for builders who are scared of screens, my brother included. I learned the hard way, from a phone at the kitchen table. I'd like to make it easier for the next person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't run. In the fast one I'd grab the first robot job going and maybe move. Here I'd stay with the co-op, build it up, and choose, rather than being chosen.

S4.say: We've been given a decade, so there's no excuse for a mess. Every worker should get paid time to retrain and the gains should be shared.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough to get good, move into the tech side and maybe teach other builders. The ending is the same, but there'd be time for the politics to catch up too.
S4.do: Gets her certificate, takes the automation course over two years and pushes the co-op to bring in robots gradually with a vote on sharing the time saved. Joins the union and local co-op network, aiming for six months of savings in five years.
S4.feel: Curious and mostly settled, with a faint unease at the very back.
S4.quote: Here I'd stay with the co-op, build it up, and choose, rather than being chosen.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Amira stops running and plans to stay, build and teach. She sees herself as a bridge for screen-averse builders like her brother. She is clear-eyed that the end point doesn't change, only her room to choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'm useless with tech, I'm the opposite, but because there's no time to use it, and Leila and I would both be hit at once. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and the robots being shared somehow, through co-ops or the public, so the people who build things still have a stake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people like me who left school early. Everyone assumes we'll be the first to go, but some of us are the ones learning fastest because we never had anyone to teach us properly. Don't write us off.

headlineQuote: Some of us are the ones learning fastest because we never had anyone to teach us properly. Don't write us off.
portrait: Amira Weber is a 27-year-old improver carpenter with a six-person eco-building co-op, renting a terrace with her bus-driver partner and holding about three weeks of savings. She left school early, uses AI every day to read drawings and revise, and sees technology as her way to catch up. She'd find a stall slightly disappointing and steady change exciting, hoping to run the site robot. The fast AGI picture makes her anxious because her edge vanishes and both she and Leila would be hit at once, while five and ten years let her plan, study automation and push the co-op to share the gains.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to use her tech skills and she and her partner would both lose work at once.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while retraining, and shared ownership of robots through co-ops or the public so builders keep a stake.
